How do I know this?...

Well, consider that their best selling console that isn't the Wii, the NES, did about 62 million units worldwide during its manufacturing period. However, like with all consoles, a significant chunk of those consoles were sold a good while after the 8-bit generation was phased out from the "big thing" in favor of 16-bit consoles. Also, while the NES dominated the American and Japanese markets for a long while, the story was different in Europe, where the Master System was the power player for that market. Also, the PC-Engine, at the time of its release, ate into the Famicom's marketshare significantly, altho at that point the Famicom had been out for so long it was inevitable.

Then there's the SNES. Yes, it sold around 49.1 million, but ask a gaffot and they'll think it did that during the 1990-1994/1995 period, which simply isn't true. SNES production ended in 1997, and unlike Sega, Nintendo actually officially supported the platform in all markets instead of killing it off early. In America, the Genesis led marketshare at 55% compared to SNES's 45% during 1992, and 65% in 1993. This dropped off during 1994, and by 1995 the SNES was leading the 16-bit console market in America. In Europe, the Mega-Drive led the market for the entirety of the official 16-bit generation. In Japan it was a different story as Super Famicom dominated that market by a healthy share even ahead of the PC-Engine, let alone the MegaDrive.

And there are periods when Sony wasn't in the console market, mind. So why bring it up? Because I'm simply illustrating that this myth gaffots (and others) believe in, that Nintendo was the Sony of gaming before Sony joined, simply never existed. They never had significant marketshare in all the major markets for their home consoles during the official span of their generations (while rival platforms were still being officially supported); the numbers speak for themselves. So seeing them sperg out with the idea the Switch can outsell PS2 (btw, 50 million or so of PS2's sales happened AFTER 360/PS3/Wii released) and its 155 million simply aren't grounded in reality. And yes, sales numbers by themselves aren't enough to describe market penetration. There's other factors too, but some of Nintendo's past tactics make their very questionable on that note. Such as how they had almost every console developer at the time working for them exclusively on NES/Famicom; that wasn't b/c those developers did it out of choice, it was because Nintendo threatened to revoke their licensing fees if they dared publish for competitor platforms. There's a good bit of info out there on it and we know Namco particularly despised them for that kind of thing (it's a huge reason why they jumped over to Sony when the PS1 came out). Then there's how they limited how many copies of games publishers could have manufactured; they laxed on this a bit w/ SNES but it was still an issue and Square was irritated a lot by that. They were also found guilty of violating anti-trust laws in 1991 and had to give rebates to NES owners as a result. So there's definitely other ways to show market penetration besides sales, but it isn't hard to find dirt on any manufacturer (Nintendo, Sony, Sega, Microsoft etc.) when doing so, either.

And to be fair, Sega did some of the same things; they also had restrictions (albeit less severe) for devs on Master System in Europe similar to how Nintendo did w/ NES in America.
